entries.topicDescription: Defining blueprints of methods, properties, and requirements.

tips.title: Protocols define contracts, not implementations
tips.content:
A protocol declares a set of methods, properties, or other
requirements that a conforming type must implement. Think of
it as a contract or a blueprint.

Unlike classes, protocols don't provide implementation by
default (though extensions can). Any struct, class, or enum
can conform to a protocol.

This is the cornerstone of protocol-oriented programming in
Swift. By coding to protocols rather than concrete types, you
make your code more flexible, testable, and composable.

A type can conform to multiple protocols, giving you the
benefits of multiple inheritance without the diamond problem.

tips.title: Protocol extensions provide default implementations
tips.content:
Swift lets you extend protocols to provide default method
implementations. Conforming types get the behavior for free
but can override it if they need something different.

This is incredibly powerful for sharing code across unrelated
types without inheritance. You define the contract in the
protocol and the shared logic in an extension.

Be careful with protocol extension dispatch: if a method is
declared in the protocol itself, dynamic dispatch kicks in.
If it's only in the extension (not required), it uses static
dispatch based on the compile-time type.

Protocol extensions are the foundation of many Swift standard
library APIs like Collection, Sequence, and Equatable.

tips.title: Use associated types for generic protocols
tips.content:
When a protocol needs to work with a generic type that
conforming types decide, use an associated type. This is
declared with 'associatedtype' inside the protocol.

Each conforming type provides a concrete type for the
associated type, either explicitly via a typealias or
implicitly through its method signatures.

Protocols with associated types cannot be used as regular
types (existentials) directly. You use them as generic
constraints with 'some' or angle-bracket syntax instead.

This pattern is used extensively in Swift: Collection has
Element, Iterator has Element, and Comparable has implicit
Self requirements.
